findings.paper_title: Appendix B Treasury Management Annual Review 2025/26
findings.headline: Financing costs ratio swung from negative to break-even, with investment income no longer offsetting borrowing costs.
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue stream shifted from -1.84% in 2024/25 (investment income exceeding borrowing costs by £635k) to 0.04% in 2025/26 (borrowing costs exceeding investment income by £10k). The council went from having surplus cash returns to near-neutral on its net external financing position.
findings.matters: This indicates the council's financial position is tightening. The loss of a cash cushion that previously offset borrowing costs signals either lower cash balances or declining investment returns, both relevant to financial resilience.
findings.figures: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream: 2024/25 Actual (1.84)%, 2025/26 Actual 0.04%; in monetary terms: (£635k) to £10k
findings.quote: Ratio of Financing Costs to Net Revenue Stream 2024/25 Actual (1.84)% 2025/26 Actual 0.04%

findings.paper_title: Appendix B Treasury Management Annual Review 2025/26
findings.headline: External debt increased by £19.4m to £84.074m following £20m Aviva borrowing in February 2026.
findings.detail: The council's total external debt rose from £64.634m (2024/25) to £84.074m (2025/26), driven by £20m of Aviva borrowing received in February 2026. The statement that 'no further borrowing required during the year' suggests the borrowing was front-loaded. Yet capital spending underperformed by £6.8m, meaning the council borrowed significantly in advance of deployment.
findings.matters: The material increase in leverage and the timing of the borrowing decision are credit-relevant. A council borrowing more than its capital spending indicates either forward-funding strategy or cash-management concerns.
findings.figures: External Debt 2024/25 £64.634m, 2025/26 £84.074m (increase £19.44m); Aviva borrowing £20m
findings.quote: £20m Aviva borrowing was received in February 2026, however there was no further borrowing required during the year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B Treasury Management Annual Review 2025/26
findings.headline: Capital expenditure significantly underspent, delivering only £34.532m against a forecast of £41.375m.
findings.detail: The council's capital programme came in £6.8m (16.6%) below forecast in 2025/26. This represents a material variance that could indicate either delivery challenges in the capital programme or over-optimistic forecasting. A council claiming to have a £41.375m capital programme but only delivering £34.532m is worth understanding.
findings.matters: Capital programme delivery is a key indicator of the council's ability to execute its financial plans. Consistent underperformance against forecast affects service investment and signals execution risk to lenders.
findings.figures: Capital Expenditure 2025/26: Estimate £41.375m, Actual £34.532m (£6.843m or 16.6% shortfall)
findings.quote: Capital Expenditure 2025/26 Estimate £41.375m Actual £34.532m

findings.headline: Housing Investment Fund is under-resourced to deliver strategic affordable housing objective.
findings.detail: The quality housing programme, a key element of capital strategy, can only deliver approximately 240 units as currently resourced and requires ongoing revenue subsidy. The council's strategic housing objective is constrained by funding availability.
findings.matters: Shows strategic objective (affordable housing) is constrained by available resources; requires ongoing revenue support that competes with other services.
findings.figures: Impact range £200–1,000k (midpoint £600k); 50% likelihood; Weighted impact £300k; Currently funded for approximately 240 units only
findings.quote: The quality housing programme, a key element of the capital programme, can only deliver social/affordable housing with the support of a revenue subsidy through the Housing Investment Fund, which is currently only funded to deliver approximately 240 units.

findings.headline: General Fund reserves stand at £17m at start of 2025/26, with £4m minimum floor policy.
findings.detail: The council operates with unallocated reserves of £17m, providing £13m above the £4m policy floor. This reserve cushion must cover unexpected costs, demographic shifts, and service pressures.
findings.matters: Reserve position determines financial resilience and flexibility; £13m above floor is modest buffer against the scale of identified risks (capital £675k, inflation £563k).
findings.figures: Unallocated General Fund reserves £17 million (as at start of 2025/26); Lower limit floor £4 million
findings.quote: At the beginning of the 2025/26 financial year unallocated General Fund reserves stood at £17 million.

findings.headline: Kent County Council's budget cuts are forcing Maidstone to find additional savings, ranked #3 risk.
findings.detail: KCC financial pressures cascade to Maidstone both directly (funding withdrawal) and indirectly (increased service demands). This creates uncontrollable external cost pressure outside Maidstone's management scope.
findings.matters: Creates uncontrollable cost pressure from external source; Maidstone has no leverage over KCC's budget decisions but faces consequences.
findings.figures: Unmitigated rating 20, mitigated rating 15; Impact range £350–750k (midpoint £550k); 75% likelihood; Weighted impact £413k
findings.quote: Budget cuts by KCC affect MBC either directly (through withdrawal of funding) or indirectly (as MBC faces increased service pressures).

findings.headline: Inflation above 2% target is the #2 ranked risk, with 75% likelihood of £500-1,000k impact.
findings.detail: Continued high inflation creates unbudgeted drain on resources beyond the council's control. If inflation runs above budget assumptions, the council may be forced to draw on reserves or cut services to balance the budget.
findings.matters: Erodes budget resilience and forces choice between service cuts or balance draw-down; external factor the council cannot control.
findings.figures: Unmitigated rating 25, mitigated rating 20; Impact range £500–1,000k (midpoint £750k); 75% likelihood; Weighted impact £563k
findings.quote: Continued high inflation will create an unbudgeted drain upon resources and the Council may not achieve its objectives without calling upon balances.

findings.headline: Budget balance depends on delivery of significant savings, with failure creating structural deficit.
findings.detail: The council's balanced budget is contingent on delivering planned savings. Non-delivery is explicitly identified as creating consequence of major scale: service suspension, redundancies. This reveals the budget has no contingency if savings plans slip.
findings.matters: If savings fail to materialize, the budget becomes unbalanced with no mitigation except cuts or reserve draw-down; shows structural dependency rather than margin.
findings.figures: Unmitigated rating 8, mitigated rating 6; Impact range £200–600k (midpoint £400k); 25% likelihood; Weighted impact £100k
findings.quote: The level of saving required to achieve a balanced budget is significant and non-delivery of these savings will have a major consequence on managing financial viability of the organisation.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation numbers are already at record levels with risk of further increase.
findings.detail: The council faces escalating costs in temporary accommodation, with numbers already at record highs and acknowledged risk of further rises. Housing benefit does not cover full costs, requiring subsidy. This is a demand-driven cost pressure the council cannot unilaterally control.
findings.matters: Structural cost pressure driven by welfare demand rather than efficiency; forces trade-offs with other services; difficult to reverse without policy change.
findings.figures: Unmitigated rating 20, mitigated rating 12; Impact range £200–1,000k (midpoint £600k); 50% likelihood; Weighted impact £300k
findings.quote: Numbers are already at record levels and there is a risk that they could increase still further.

findings.headline: Capital programme delivery is the #1 ranked budget risk, with £600-1,200k potential impact.
findings.detail: The council depends on multiple funding sources (internal borrowing, PWLB, capital grants, developer contributions) to deliver its capital programme. Loss or reduction of these sources is the highest-ranked financial risk by weighted impact and likelihood. Even after existing controls, the risk remains severe.
findings.matters: Capital programme delivery drives strategic objectives and economic growth; constrained funding forces prioritization or suspension of schemes, delaying economic benefit and creating delivery risk.
findings.figures: Unmitigated rating 25, mitigated rating 20; Impact range £600–1,200k (midpoint £900k); 75% likelihood; Weighted impact £675k
findings.quote: Reduction or total loss of funding sources means that the capital programme cannot be delivered or demands on funding exceed available supply

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account opening requiring new governance and financial arrangements
findings.detail: The council is preparing to open a Housing Revenue Account, which requires constitutional changes and implementation of new governance structures. This represents a significant structural change to how the council manages housing finances.
findings.matters: Opening an HRA is a major structural change that separates housing finances from the general fund, requiring new financial management systems and potentially indicating a shift in housing strategy or demand response.
findings.figures: n/a
findings.quote: As well as planning for implementing appropriate governance arrangements for opening the Housing Revenue Account.

findings.headline: Local Government Reorganisation creates significant delivery risk alongside acute financial pressures
findings.detail: The council identifies LGR as one of its biggest challenges, requiring simultaneous delivery of key priorities and business as usual while preparing for reorganisation. The council notes financial pressures across local government remain acute, demand continues to rise, and uncertainty is increasing. Maintaining capacity to deliver transformation and business as usual is flagged as a key priority.
findings.matters: A major structural reorganisation creates execution risk: the council must maintain service delivery and financial discipline while managing transformation, potentially straining leadership focus and resources at a time of acute budget pressure.
findings.figures: n/a
findings.quote: Financial pressures across local government remain acute, demand for services continues to rise, and there is increasing uncertainty linked to the potential for local government reorganisation.

findings.headline: External auditor required establishment of long-term savings programme
findings.detail: Grant Thornton's 2024/25 value-for-money report recommended the council establish a long-term savings programme, indicating the auditor identified sustained budget pressures requiring multi-year corrective action. The council has actioned this recommendation.
findings.matters: An external auditor recommendation to establish a long-term savings programme signals the council faces identified structural budget gaps or sustainability concerns that require discipline across multiple years.
findings.figures: One improvement recommendation in Grant Thornton's 2024/25 report
findings.quote: one improvement recommendation was made by the External Auditor in relation to the establishment of a long-term savings programme which has been actioned.

findings.headline: Housing Rents audit received weak assurance rating with 37 audit findings
findings.detail: Internal audit assessed housing rental income controls and found deficiencies in design and operation affecting rent setting, collection, reconciliation, reporting, and income protection. The findings total 3 high-priority, 13 medium-priority and 21 low-priority items. Controls must be developed and embedded in the new housing management service.
findings.matters: A weak rating in rental income controls indicates material risk of uncollected revenue and exposure to fraud, directly affecting the council's cash flow and financial sustainability.
findings.figures: 37 findings total: 3 High, 13 Medium, 21 Low
findings.quote: The audit was assessed with a weak assurance rating meaning that controls within the service have deficiencies in their design and operation that leave it exposed to uncontrolled operational risk with a potential failure to achieve key service aims.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Housing Benefit Subsidy Claim 2024/25
findings.headline: Reconciliation variance of £1,325.88 in backdated expenditure identified but left unamended
findings.detail: Auditors identified a discrepancy between the Housing Benefit Subsidy Claim Form and the council's supporting reports for backdated expenditure (Cell 038): the form showed £0 while the reports showed £1,325.88. The variance indicates inconsistent recording, and the council made no amendments to resolve it.
findings.matters: An unresolved audit variance suggests incomplete controls over reconciliation and data integrity in the benefits system
findings.figures: £1,325.88 variance between claim form (£0) and subsidy reports (£1,325.88)
findings.quote: We reconciled headline cells and associated detailed cells to the Local Authority's Final Subsidy Reports and identified a variance of £1,325.88 between the Claim Form (MPF720A) and the supporting reports.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Housing Benefit Subsidy Claim 2024/25
findings.headline: Auditors found 5 housing benefit cases misclassified between expenditure cells, indicating control weaknesses not caught internally
findings.detail: Accommodation was incorrectly classified as self-contained (Cell 014) instead of non-self-contained (Cell 012) in 5 cases totalling £3,032.30 in errors. Initial testing found one case triggering additional testing of 40 more cases, which found four further errors. When extrapolated to the full population of 455 cases in Cell 014, this creates a £28,440 adjustment.
findings.matters: The pattern of misclassification errors—missed by the council and only found through audit testing—indicates control weaknesses in housing benefit processing
findings.figures: 5 claims with £3,032.30 direct errors; £28,440 population-level adjustment; 2.07% error rate in the Cell 014 population of 455 cases
findings.quote: 5 claims (total case value £7,225.55) were discovered to have been classified in Cell 014 rather than Cell 012, resulting in an overstatement of Cell 014 and a corresponding understatement of Cell 012 totalling £3,032.30.

findings.headline: Successor unitary authority will inherit significant budget gaps from Medway and Kent authorities
findings.detail: Maidstone will be abolished in April 2028 and merged into West Kent Unitary with Tonbridge & Malling, Tunbridge Wells, and Sevenoaks. The paper flags that the incoming unitary's finances are compromised: 'Kent County Council and Medway Council together account for 87% of the 14 existing authorities' net revenue and already face significant budget gaps. Medway Council is one of 30 authorities from around the country that have been granted 'Exceptional Financial Support' (EFS) by the government in 2025/26 in order to manage financial pressures.'
findings.matters: Lenders to the successor authority will inherit pre-existing budget gaps and authorities already in financial support; reorganisation savings may not materialise and could be delayed.
findings.figures: 87% of 14 authorities' revenue is held by Kent CC and Medway; Medway one of 30 nationally receiving Exceptional Financial Support in 2025/26.
findings.quote: Kent County Council and Medway Council together account for 87% of the 14 existing authorities' net revenue and already face significant budget gaps. Medway Council is one of 30 authorities from around the country that have been granted 'Exceptional Financial Support' (EFS) by the government in 2025/26 in order to manage financial pressures.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs spiking again after Miller Heights evacuation in May 2026
findings.detail: The council overspent significantly on temporary accommodation in 2025/26 but expected this to reverse. However, the private evacuation of Miller Heights residential tower block in May 2026 has created a new pressure: 'some of the families made homeless through the evacuation of the privately owned Miller Heights residential tower block in May 2026 currently being accommodated by the Council.'
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation was a material overspend in the prior year; new forced displacement is creating unbudgeted ongoing costs.
findings.figures: 2025/26 temporary accommodation overspend (amount not specified but noted as significant).
findings.quote: There remains however a risk of temporary accommodation costs increasing again, with some of the families made homeless through the evacuation of the privately owned Miller Heights residential tower block in May 2026 currently being accommodated by the Council.

findings.headline: Social housing programme second tranche (332 units) depends on Homes England grant decision
findings.detail: First tranche of 83 units is under construction and funded. The next phase of 332 units at Maidstone East and Springfield Library 'is subject to a funding bid to Homes England, to be submitted shortly. The delivery of these units as social/affordable housing depends on the outcome of this bid.' Without this grant, the council cannot justify the investment under prudential borrowing rules.
findings.matters: A major capital programme component is dependent on external government grant approval, creating delivery risk for a council approaching dissolution.
findings.figures: First tranche: 83 units under construction. Second tranche: 332 units pending Homes England funding bid.
findings.quote: The next tranche of 332 units, including the developments at Maidstone East and Springfield Library, is subject to a funding bid to Homes England, to be submitted shortly. The delivery of these units as social/affordable housing depends on the outcome of this bid.

findings.headline: Borrowing costs have tripled, threatening capital programme delivery
findings.detail: The council locked in £80 million of borrowing at 2.87% in 2022 (final tranche drawn February 2026). Any further borrowing required for its ambitious capital programme (£39m in 2026/27, £234m over five years) faces rates of 6.2% for 50-year PWLB loans. The council warns this creates 'a correspondingly high threshold for demonstrating a business case for future capital expenditure, thus putting at risk the Council's capacity to deliver the capital programme while remaining within the prudential borrowing rules.'
findings.matters: Rising borrowing costs directly threaten the council's ability to deliver its capital programme while staying within prudential limits, affecting both council projects and social housing delivery.
findings.figures: Locked rate: 2.87%; Current 50-year PWLB: 6.2%. Capital programme: £39m (2026/27), £234m (five years).
findings.quote: The cost of 50 year Public Works Loan Board borrowing at the time of writing is 6.2%. This means a correspondingly high threshold for demonstrating a business case for future capital expenditure, thus putting at risk the Council's capacity to deliver the capital programme while remaining within the prudential borrowing rules.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025/26
findings.headline: Phishing attack exploited incomplete multi-factor authentication deployment despite audit findings on ICT access controls
findings.detail: Following completion of the ICT Controls audit, the council experienced a phishing attack that compromised an officer's email account. The audit had identified that multi-factor authentication was not consistently applied to all staff accounts despite being a mandatory requirement, and some accounts were only locked down after the incident occurred.
findings.matters: Shows that identified control weaknesses in the control environment may not be fully remediated in practice; information security incidents could lead to data loss, operational disruption, or breach of confidential borrowing/financial information.
findings.figures: No financial figures; MFA requirement not fully applied
findings.quote: Since our work concluded, Maidstone Borough Council have been subject to a phishing attack as a result of access being gained to an officer's e-mail account. There is a requirement for MFA to be applied to all staff accounts, however there were a few instances where this has not been applied as expected.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025/26
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation costs flagged as strategic budget risk; council implementing mitigation with predicted savings targets
findings.detail: The council reported temporary accommodation costs as a strategic budget risk in November 2025. It is reducing reliance on nightly B&B accommodation through increased use of council-owned stock (MBC stock, Trinity House, Marsham Street) with projected savings of £174k in 2026/27 and £149k in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Rising homelessness demand is creating cost pressures that require ongoing mitigation; a lender would need to monitor whether the savings targets are being achieved and whether this pressure continues to grow.
findings.figures: £174k predicted saving 2026/27; £149k predicted saving 2027/28
findings.quote: Temporary accommodation costs were reported as a strategic budget risk to the Audit, Governance and Standards Committee in November 2025 where it was recognised the increased use of MBC stock, Trinity House and Marsham Street (a policy informed by trend analysis and insight) is reducing reliance on nightly B&B and the inherent costs with predicted savings of £174k in 2026/27 and £149k in 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Enc. 1 for Internal Audit Annual Report and Opinion 2025/26
findings.headline: Housing Rents service rated Weak with 37 findings, citing control deficiencies in governance and record management
findings.detail: The Housing Rents audit identified weak controls across a revenue-generating function, with 3 high-priority, 13 medium, and 21 low-priority actions. The audit found governance and control arrangements have not kept pace with operational change, with reliance on informal practices and poor information management affecting service delivery and control compliance.
findings.matters: Housing rental income is a material revenue stream; weak controls over income management and record-keeping create risk of financial inaccuracy and potential debt management failures.
findings.figures: 37 findings: 3 high-priority, 13 medium, 21 low-priority actions
findings.quote: For 2025/26 a key area of concern has been identified in the Housing Service. The have been a number of themes borne out of our audit work, such as governance and control arrangements not keeping pace with operational change, reliance on informal working practices and individual knowledge, poor information and record management and service delivery priorities influencing control compliance.

findings.headline: Council acquiring units after Registered Providers declined to take the Section 106 affordable housing
findings.detail: The council states that Registered Providers declined to acquire the affordable housing units secured through Section 106 planning obligations. The council is stepping in to acquire these units 'in response to market failure' where the private social housing sector would not take them on, ensuring the affordable units are not lost.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand when a council is taking on housing acquisition deals that registered providers have rejected, as this signals difficult market conditions or risk factors in housing delivery
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: The acquisition is necessary in response to market failure to secure the delivery of much needed affordable housing in the borough.

findings.headline: Council deploying capital programme funding to acquire affordable housing units with expected rate of return
findings.detail: Maidstone is acquiring affordable housing units via a development agreement as part of its capital programme. The paper explicitly states that the investment will produce a positive financial effect through a 'rate of return.' The acquisition is funded from existing capital programme resources and the council expects this to deliver financial benefits alongside housing provision.
findings.matters: This represents material capital deployment with explicit financial return expectations, indicating the council's capital strategy and risk appetite for housing investments
findings.figures: No specific acquisition cost, number of units, or rate of return disclosed in public sections (contained in exempt Appendix 3)
findings.quote: Overall, for finance there will be a positive effect, as the already identified investment in the capital programme will produce a rate of return.

findings.headline: Council is delivering major new initiatives and spending £2.9m in new priorities while preparing for local government reorganisation, stretching organizational capacity
findings.detail: The council has committed to delivering £900k in new budget allocations and reallocating £2.3m from earmarked reserves to fund spending priorities including economic development, nature recovery, climate change, and a healthy living centre feasibility study. The report explicitly states this work 'places heavy demands on the capacity of the organisation, at a time when it is preparing for local government reorganisation'—a significant institutional change.
findings.matters: Stretched organizational capacity during a major institutional transition creates risk of project delivery failures, budget overruns, and management distraction from core financial controls
findings.figures: New spending: £900k from budget + £2.3m from earmarked reserves; Economic Development £1.5m; Major works to assets £500k
findings.quote: this work places heavy demands on the capacity of the organisation, at a time when it is preparing for local government reorganisation.

findings.headline: Council identifies inflation risks have grown since February 2026 due to Middle East instability, at a time when reserves are already tight
findings.detail: Reserves were reviewed in February 2026 and inflation was noted as a risk. By July, the council reports that 'the risks facing the Council have grown in magnitude', explicitly citing Middle East instability as keeping inflation at current levels or likely to increase further. This is material because the council had just concluded that reserves were 'adequate but not excessive' in light of the risks faced.
findings.matters: Continued inflation erodes the real value of budgets and reserves while increasing capital programme costs and service pressures, constraining the council's ability to absorb future shocks
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves £36.6m; general fund balance £17.3m
findings.quote: Since reserves were reviewed in February 2026, the risks facing the Council have grown in magnitude. The continuing instability in the Middle East means that inflation is likely to remain at current levels or even increase.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation overspent in 2025/26 and recent evacuation has spiked numbers again, creating ongoing cost risk
findings.detail: The council experienced a significant overspend on temporary accommodation for homeless families in 2025/26, forming part of a £586k overspend in the Housing and Community Cohesion budget. Although a downward trend appeared in Q4 2025/26, the recent evacuation of Miller Heights has reversed this and increased the number of households in temporary accommodation again. The council identifies this as an ongoing risk and notes uncertainty about how long the spike will last.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a statutory obligation with volatile demand and costs that cannot easily be controlled; recent shocks suggest budget pressure could return despite Q4 improvement
findings.figures: Housing and Community Cohesion overspend £586k in 2025/26; £4.882m actual spend against £4.295m budget
findings.quote: The recent evacuation of Miller Heights has led to an increase in the numbers in temporary accommodation. It remains too soon to say how long term this increase will be, but this event has highlighted the continuing risk of additional costs in meeting the Council's housing obligations.

findings.headline: Council has not yet secured Homes England funding for next phase of affordable housing, risking pressure to increase its own subsidy
findings.detail: The council planned its affordable housing delivery with anticipated Homes England funding for the next phase. This funding has not yet been secured. If it is not forthcoming, the council will need to increase its own subsidy through the Housing Investment Fund beyond currently set-aside money, creating an unfunded liability. The council is addressing this by allocating £409k of the underspend to the fund.
findings.matters: Unplanned housing subsidy requirements reduce financial flexibility and would increase pressure on reserves or borrowing requirements at a time when reserves are already assessed as adequate but not excessive
findings.figures: Housing Investment Fund £15.5 million; allocation of £409k from underspend
findings.quote: The Council has not yet secured funding from Homes England for the next phase of the social / affordable housing programme. Insufficient funding could put pressure on the council to increase its own level of subsidy through the Housing Investment Fund, above and beyond money already set aside or planned to be set aside, in order to enable delivery of the programme.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E1: Treasury Management Strategy for 2026/27
findings.headline: Borrowing strategy bets on interest rate falls and reserves the right to borrow aggressively if rates rise faster than forecast.
findings.detail: The council is maintaining an under-borrowed position with £80m of forward borrowing already locked in, betting that PWLB rates will fall. The strategy reserves discretion to undertake additional 'forward borrowing whilst interest rates are lower' if rates rise faster than the MUFG forecast. This creates execution risk: if rates spike or the capital program accelerates, the council may be forced into emergency borrowing at unfavourable terms.
findings.matters: Market-timing borrowing strategies are vulnerable to forecast error; a wrong call on interest rates can force a council into significantly higher debt costs or force capital deferrals at short notice.
findings.figures: Current under-borrowing position: 2026/27 £42.368m; 2027/28 £51.660m; 2028/29 £53.758m. Current PWLB rates (22 Dec 2025): 5-year 4.81%, 10-year 5.39%.
findings.quote: if it was felt that there was a significant risk of a much sharper RISE in borrowing rates than that currently forecast, consideration will be given to further forward borrowing whilst interest rates are lower than they are projected to be in the next few years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix E1: Treasury Management Strategy for 2026/27
findings.headline: Financing cost ratio jumps from 0.49% to 12.16% of net revenue over five years, signalling mounting affordability strain.
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs (interest and capital charges) to revenue stream increases more than 25-fold, from 0.49% in 2025/26 to 8.01% in 2027/28 and peaking at 12.16% in 2029/30. This rapid deterioration reflects both the growing capital program and rising borrowing commitments, creating sustained pressure on the revenue budget's flexibility to fund services or maintain reserves.
findings.matters: Financing cost ratios above 8–10% are a warning sign in local authority lending; they indicate the council is absorbing increasing debt costs that crowd out service provision and limit financial headroom.
findings.quote: This indicator identifies the trend in the cost of capital, (borrowing and other long-term obligation costs net of investment income), against the net revenue stream. 2025/26 0.49%, 2026/27 4.37%, 2027/28 8.01%, 2028/29 10.21%, 2029/30 12.16%

findings.paper_title: Appendix E1: Treasury Management Strategy for 2026/27
findings.headline: Maidstone faces a funding gap by 2027/28 with capital needs of £194m but only £85m of borrowing locked in.
findings.detail: The council's Capital Financing Requirement grows to £194.1m by 2027/28, while external debt only reaches £142.5m—leaving under-borrowing of £51.7m. The strategy acknowledges this gap explicitly, noting that 'if it meets the prudential criteria' further borrowing will proceed, otherwise 'the capital spending profile of the council will be adjusted to defer investment until such time as it is affordable.' This signals potential project deferrals.
findings.matters: A funding gap forces a council into either aggressive market-timed borrowing or deferred capital investment. Either outcome constrains the lender's understanding of the council's true capital trajectory and financial resilience.
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement 2027/28: £194.146m. External Debt 2027/28: £142.486m. Under-borrowing: £51.660m. Only £85m locked in from forward needs.
findings.quote: At present, the Council has only locked in £85 million of borrowing (£5m PWLB and £80m market loans), leaving a gap between the liability benchmark and borrowing from as early as 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.headline: High interest rates identified as a risk to the ability to deliver the capital programme
findings.detail: The council identifies among key budget risks that 'Continued high interest rates will impact the Council's ability to deliver its capital programme ambitions.' This indicates the council is already constrained by financing costs on its £232m capital investment plan.
findings.matters: This suggests that further interest rate rises could force the council to scale back or delay capital projects, affecting delivery of its corporate strategy.
findings.figures: None specified
findings.quote: Continued high interest rates will impact the Council's ability to deliver its capital programme ambitions.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility income of £2.7m in 2026/27 will decline to £0.5m by 2030/31
findings.detail: A new income stream from packaging-related levies contributes £2.7m in 2026/27 but is projected to decline sharply as producers meet waste-reduction targets. The council assumes payments will fall to £0.5m by 2030/31, representing a £2.2m loss of income over the five-year period.
findings.matters: The council's financial projections rely on declining income from a source explicitly designed to reduce. This is not a sustainable revenue base and masks the underlying structural deficit.
findings.quote: Payments in future years are likely to reduce, assuming that the levy successfully incentivises producers to reduce the volume of packaging.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.headline: Local government reorganisation is planned for April 2028, but the timetable 'could slip', leaving unresolved deficits
findings.detail: The council's financial strategy assumes the planned merger into a unitary authority will proceed in 2028/29. However, it acknowledges this timetable could slip. If reorganisation does not proceed and the 2027/28 deficit persists, it 'could become an ongoing challenge for the Council' with 'no clear remedy' other than continued reserves depletion.
findings.matters: This creates material planning uncertainty. If LGR is delayed, the council faces a structural deficit with no identified solution, posing risk to its long-term viability.
findings.figures: 2028 assumed date; 2027/28 deficit unresolved if LGR slips
findings.quote: As a result, a budget deficit in 2027/28 for which there is no clear remedy could become an ongoing challenge for the Council if reorganisation is not implemented.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.headline: Housing Investment Fund requires £8m revenue subsidy over two years before opening HRA
findings.detail: The council is allocating £4m in 2026/27 and £4m in 2027/28 from revenue to the Housing Investment Fund. This subsidy is necessary because social housing revenue is insufficient to cover borrowing costs; the council assumes £50,000 per unit must be set aside from revenue. This subsidy commitment creates the projected 2027/28 deficit.
findings.matters: This large and ongoing revenue commitment limits financial flexibility and demonstrates that the housing programme cannot sustain itself from its own rental income — it is dependent on council subsidy.
findings.figures: £8m total; £4m 2026/27; £4m 2027/28; £50,000 per unit subsidy assumption
findings.quote: It has been assumed for planning purposes that a capital sum of £50,000 per unit must be set aside from revenue expenditure for each completed unit of social/affordable housing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.headline: Five-year capital programme of £232m requires additional borrowing beyond the existing £80m facility, at higher cost
findings.detail: The council has an £80m forward borrowing facility with Aviva at 2.87%, of which £60m has been drawn. The capital programme totals £232m (including £144m for housing), requiring substantial new borrowing from 2026/27 onwards. The council explicitly states this additional borrowing will be 'at a higher cost than existing borrowing'.
findings.matters: Rising debt servicing costs from higher-rate borrowing will add to revenue pressure. As the cheap £80m facility is exhausted, future debt costs may become unaffordable without further savings or income growth.
findings.figures: £232m total capital programme; £144m housing; £80m facility at 2.87%; £60m drawn to date
findings.quote: Additional borrowing, above and beyond the scheduled £80 million, will therefore be required, starting in 2026/27. This is likely to be at a higher cost than existing borrowing.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.headline: Budget deficits of £0.9m in 2027/28 and £1.6m in 2030/31, to be covered by drawing down reserves
findings.detail: Revenue projections show deficits emerging in years two and five of the strategy. The 2027/28 deficit (£0.9m net after savings) arises from £8m Housing Investment Fund contributions; the 2030/31 deficit from costs of funding capital expenditure. The council states reserves are 'sufficient to allow their use for the purpose of smoothing the profile'.
findings.matters: Planned reserve drawdown indicates the council's recurring revenue cannot cover its spending plans. This signals weakening financial sustainability and reduces the buffer available for unforeseen pressures.
findings.figures: £1.5m gross deficit 2027/28; £0.9m net deficit; £1.6m deficit 2030/31
findings.quote: it is considered that the level of reserves is sufficient to allow their use for the purpose of smoothing the profile set out and balancing the budget.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.headline: All business rates growth since 2013/14 has been reset and lost under the new funding settlement
findings.detail: The council previously benefited from retaining business rates growth in Maidstone. Under Fair Funding, this entire accumulated benefit has been wiped, resetting the baseline. The council now retains only 8.2% (£6.2m) of total business rates income of £75.8m.
findings.matters: This represents loss of a material and previously reliable income stream, reducing financial flexibility precisely when funding is most constrained.
findings.figures: 8.2% retention (£6.2m out of £75.8m total); growth from 2013/14 now lost
findings.quote: Assumed business rates income has been reset, such that business rates growth since 2013/14, from which the Council has hitherto benefitted, has been lost.

findings.paper_title: Appendix G: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27 to 2030/31
findings.headline: Core Spending Power growing at only 1.6% per annum, below inflation, creating a real-terms funding cut
findings.detail: The new 'Fair Funding' regime rebalances resources away from shire districts. Maidstone's CSP increases of 1.6% annually fall well short of inflation, meaning the council's resources are declining in real terms. This puts the council on a constrained trajectory over the next five years.
findings.matters: A lender assessing municipal sustainability must understand that the council faces structural funding pressure with no growth headroom to manage spending inflation or service pressures.
findings.figures: 1.6% per annum; inflation forecast 2.5% for 2026/27
findings.quote: Maidstone's CSP is projected to grow by just 1.6% per annum over the next five years, which is less than the likely future rate of inflation.

findings.headline: The council has already committed to £80m of long-term borrowing from Aviva Life & Pensions UK at 2.87%, received in three tranches through February 2026.
findings.detail: The council secured this facility to fund capital expenditure ahead of interest rate increases. The three tranches (£40m Feb 2024, £20m Feb 2025, £20m Feb 2026) are already committed and largely drawn. This locks in cost at a time when PWLB rates are higher.
findings.matters: The council has front-loaded borrowing and tied up its debt facilities early. Future capital schemes will face higher rates if further external borrowing is needed, or will need to be funded from constrained internal resources or external grants.
findings.figures: £80m total facility at 2.87%; £60m drawn by end of February 2025; final £20m in February 2026.
findings.quote: the Council secured £80m of long term borrowing through Aviva Life & Pensions UK Limited to fund the increasing capital programme at a cost of 2.87%. The first tranche totalling £40m was received in February 2024, the second £20m in February 2025 and the remaining £20m in February 2026.

findings.headline: The council acknowledges that budget gaps in future years are "much more challenging" and will require "a more radical approach."
findings.detail: Section 2.13 states that while 2026/27 has a proposed solution to the budget gap, "the position in future years is much more challenging and will require a more radical approach." No detail is given on what this approach might be, what the gaps are, or when the council will need to act.
findings.matters: This is a tacit admission that current budget plans are inadequate beyond 2026/27. Vague references to "radical approach" without specification suggest the council has not yet developed credible plans to balance the medium-term financial strategy. Lenders need to understand what savings or revenue-raising the council plans and whether they are achievable.
findings.figures: No specific gap figures provided for post-2026/27 years.
findings.quote: The position in future years is much more challenging and will require a more radical approach.

findings.headline: Financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream will rise to 12.1% by 2030/31—a 24-fold increase from 0.5% in 2025/26.
findings.detail: The council's revenue budget will be consumed increasingly by interest and MRP (minimum revenue provision) on capital borrowing. By 2030/31, one pound in every eight of available revenue will go to servicing past capital decisions. This trajectory leaves progressively less room for service delivery.
findings.matters: A lender assesses ability to repay and revenue resilience. Rapid growth in financing costs is a warning signal that the council is committing more of its revenue stream to historic decisions, reducing its flexibility to absorb shocks or meet changing service demands.
findings.figures: Financing costs 2025/26: £0.185m (0.494% of net revenue stream). By 2030/31: £4.905m (12.115% of net revenue stream).

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement projected to rise by £209m (139%) over ten years, reaching £353.6m by 2035/36.
findings.detail: Debt is forecast to grow from £84.1m (March 2026) to £320.3m (March 2036). External borrowing over the ten-year period totals £236.2m against £400.6m of capital expenditure. The council will rely on borrowing to cover 59% of all capital spending; external sources cover only 35% and own resources just 6%.
findings.matters: Rapid debt accumulation reduces future borrowing capacity, increases exposure to interest rate risk, and narrows the buffer between actual debt and the legal affordable borrowing limit. By 2035/36, debt approaches the CFR ceiling, with little room for additional borrowing.
findings.figures: CFR growth: £118.9m (2025/26) to £353.6m (2035/36). Total external borrowing planned: £236.2m. Debt forecast: £320.3m by March 2036.
findings.quote: The CFR is expected to increase by £209m over the next 10 years.

findings.headline: The £196.9m Quality Homes program cannot be justified under prudential borrowing rules and requires £50,000 of revenue subsidy per unit.
findings.detail: The council states explicitly that homes let at social or affordable levels cannot meet the financial viability test required for prudential borrowing. It therefore requires subsidy from revenue spending. The council has calculated a £50,000-per-unit subsidy and is building a Housing Investment Fund to absorb this. A further £8 million must be transferred to the HIF in two tranches (£4m in 2026/27, £4m in 2027/28) to fund homes already in the pipeline.
findings.matters: This is the single largest element of capital expenditure (£196.9m over ten years, £139.5m in five years). The fact that it is economically unviable and requires ongoing revenue support signals a long-term structural demand that will crowd revenue spending, reducing the council's financial resilience.
findings.figures: Quality Homes for Life: £196.9m over ten years, £139.5m in first five years. Subsidy rate: £50,000 per unit. Additional HIF transfer required: £8 million total.
findings.quote: As the proposed new homes will be let at social or affordable levels, the necessary investment cannot be justified under the prudential borrowing rules. Instead, an element of subsidy is required, both from external sources (Homes England) and the Council's own revenue expenditure.

findings.headline: Maidstone will be absorbed into a new unitary authority in April 2028/29.
findings.detail: The council acknowledges this absorption as expected and proceeds with five-year planning on the assumption it will occur. The document notes it is "good practice" to continue five-year financial planning despite this. No analysis of transition risk or impact on borrowing capacity is offered.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether this creates refinancing risk, whether the successor authority will honour the council's borrowings, and whether capital commitments made now will still be binding after merger.
findings.figures: Planned absorption 2028/29; five-year capital plan extends to 2030/31 and ten-year plan to 2035/36.
findings.quote: It is expected that Maidstone Borough Council will be absorbed in a new unitary authority with effect from 2028/29 as part of local government reorganisation. However, it is good practice to continue planning over a five-year cycle.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Final Saving Proposals and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Business Rates Pool dissolved due to reset in government funding, removing income smoothing mechanism
findings.detail: The council and nine other Kent authorities are ending their pooling arrangement because the funding reset has eliminated the surplus income that made pooling worthwhile. This removes a source of income flexibility.
findings.matters: The council loses a mechanism for managing volatility in business rates income and becomes fully exposed to collection risk and reset cycles.
findings.figures: Pool of Kent County Council plus 9 districts ending
findings.quote: Kent County Council and the nine Kent districts that formed a Business Rates Pool in 2025/26 have agreed to stop the pooling their business rates growth, as the government's review of local government funding has reset local authorities' share of business rates and little or no surplus is expected

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Final Saving Proposals and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Fundamental governance uncertainty: council facing potential subsumption into unitary authority in 2028/29
findings.detail: The council's entire medium-term budget strategy is built on the assumption that it will be merged into a new unitary authority by 2028/29. This is not yet certain and creates planning uncertainty for both the council and its creditors.
findings.matters: A lender must understand that the council's structure and thus creditworthiness may change materially within the planning horizon, and the budget plan depends on that change.
findings.quote: the budget can be brought back into balance by the time that Maidstone Borough Council is potentially subsumed into a new unitary authority in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Final Saving Proposals and Capital Programme
findings.headline: £234m capital programme over five years requires £131m of prudential borrowing
findings.detail: The council is pursuing a significant capital programme funded primarily through borrowing, with revenue financing costs reflected in the treasury strategy but exposed to interest rate risk.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the scale of the council's debt issuance and whether revenues can servicedebt if interest rates or scope shift again.
findings.figures: £234m capital programme; £131m prudential borrowing
findings.quote: The proposals set out in this report indicate a need for up to £131 million of prudential borrowing over the lifetime of the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Final Saving Proposals and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Medway Bridge capital project budget more than doubled from £1.75m to £4m with minimal explanation
findings.detail: The council has revised the bridge project budget upward by £2.25m (128% increase) in this round of budget setting. The paper attributes this only to 'latest understanding of likely costs' without specifying what changed or why.
findings.matters: A major unexplained cost escalation on a named capital scheme signals either scope drift, inflation exposure, or estimation weakness on this project.
findings.quote: The main change relates to the Medway Bridge project which formerly had a proposed budget of £1.75m, which is now being increased to £4m to reflect the latest understanding of likely costs.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Final Saving Proposals and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Council projects a budget deficit in 2027/28, relying on earmarked reserves to plug it
findings.detail: Despite a balanced 2026/27 budget, the council forecasts a deficit for 2027/28 and explicitly states it will use the earmarked future funding pressures reserve to manage the gap. The underlying position only recovers if the council is absorbed into a unitary authority in 2028/29.
findings.matters: The council cannot currently solve a medium-term structural deficit without drawing reserves or assuming an external governance change.
findings.figures: Deficit in 2027/28; recovery by 2028/29 pending reorganisation
findings.quote: the medium term position is that, while a deficit is projected for 2027/28, the budget can be brought back into balance by the time that Maidstone Borough Council is potentially subsumed into a new unitary authority in 2028/29.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Strategy and Final Saving Proposals and Capital Programme
findings.headline: Core Spending Power rising below inflation, creating structural real-terms funding squeeze
findings.detail: The new Fair Funding settlement increases annual spending power by 0.8–1.7%, below the assumed inflation rate. This is a phased three-year transition in which Maidstone's funding will decline because its existing level exceeds the new Settlement Funding Assessment.
findings.matters: A lender and finance director need to know the council faces structural resource contraction, not temporary pressure.
findings.quote: the annual increase in Core Spending Power is less than the likely rate of inflation, meaning a real terms decrease in spending power.

news_drafts.headline: Financing costs ratio swung from negative to break-even, with investment income no longer offsetting borrowing costs.
news_drafts.lead: This indicates the council's financial position is tightening. The loss of a cash cushion that previously offset borrowing costs signals either lower cash balances or declining investment returns, both relevant to financial resilience.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix B Treasury Management Annual Review 2025/26

news_drafts.headline: External debt increased by £19.4m to £84.074m following £20m Aviva borrowing in February 2026.
news_drafts.lead: The material increase in leverage and the timing of the borrowing decision are credit-relevant. A council borrowing more than its capital spending indicates either forward-funding strategy or cash-management concerns.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix B Treasury Management Annual Review 2025/26

news_drafts.headline: Capital expenditure significantly underspent, delivering only £34.532m against a forecast of £41.375m.
news_drafts.lead: Capital programme delivery is a key indicator of the council's ability to execute its financial plans. Consistent underperformance against forecast affects service investment and signals execution risk to lenders.
news_drafts.paper_title: Appendix B Treasury Management Annual Review 2025/26
